source: Stab & Gurevych (2017) Parsing argumentation structures in persuasive essays
finding: Annotation scheme for essays: major claim, claim, premise, with support and attack relations. Argument structure is modelled as a tree, so divergent structure and cycles are excluded by design.
numbers: Corpus: 402 persuasive essays from essayforum.com; 6,089 components (751 major claims, 1,506 claims, 3,832 premises). 80 essays annotated by three annotators, 322 by one expert.
limits: Tree assumption ignores divergent arguments; one cited study found 5.26% divergent arguments in political speeches. Essays are a clean, claim-first genre.
agent_relevance: Standard pipeline for S1/S2: find components first, then relations, then stance. A tree restatement (one claim, grounds beneath) is a defensible default.

source: Stab & Gurevych (2017) Parsing argumentation structures in persuasive essays
finding: Humans agree well on major claims and premises, less on plain claims.
numbers: Fleiss kappa: major claim .877 (agreement 97.9%), claim .635 (88.9%), premise .833 (91.6%). Krippendorff unitized alpha: .810, .524, .824. Relations: support kappa .708, attack kappa .737. Annotators marked only 0.9% of 4,922 pairs as attack and 18.4% as support.
limits: Sentence-level kappa is an approximation; 4.3% of sentences held several components. Claim boundary is the weak point (alpha .524).
agent_relevance: Even trained humans split on what counts as a claim versus a premise. The agent should not treat its own claim/premise labels as ground truth; check by a rule.

source: Stab & Gurevych (2017) Parsing argumentation structures in persuasive essays
finding: Supervised plus integer linear programming (ILP) joint model parses components, relations and stance. Close to human on components, further on relations and stance.
numbers: Test F1 (80 essays): human upper bound .868 components, .854 relations, .844 stance. ILP joint model .826 components, .751 relations, .680 stance. Heuristic baseline .759, .700, .562. Model reaches 95.2% of human on components, 87.9% relations, 80.5% stance. Linked-pair F1 gain +.077 from joint model; claim F1 +.071. Attack stance F1 only .413.
limits: Pre-LLM; essays only. Microtext check: ILP component F1 .857, relation .683, stance .745.
agent_relevance: Components are nearly solved; relation and attack stance are the hard part. Restating grounds is easier than judging whether they attack.

source: Stab & Gurevych (2017) Parsing argumentation structures in persuasive essays
finding: Linked versus convergent: the authors argue the distinction need not be made when identifying structure. Linked arguments (premises relevant only together; Thomas 1973) differ from convergent ones (each premise supports alone; Beardsley 1950). The split is ambiguous in real text.
numbers: Cites Freeman (2011) that the traditional definition is ambiguous in everyday talk; Yanal (1991): linked/convergent equals one versus several arguments; Conway (1991): linked can be omitted.
limits: Theory remains disputed. Their stance is a modelling choice, not a proof.
agent_relevance: A schema may keep structure as a plain tree and decide linkage later, in a separate check (see the removal test in the Davies chapter).
quote: The question if an argumentation model needs to distinguish between linked and convergent arguments is still debated in argumentation theory

source: Lawrence & Reed (2019) Argument Mining: A Survey
finding: Survey defines convergent (premises support independently; removing one does not weaken the others), linked (premises each need the others), and divergent (one premise, several conclusions). Notes Toulmin is widely used and Freeman gives the clearest synthesis for computing. Many tools force a tree and so cannot show divergent structure.
numbers: AIFdb holds over 14,000 Argument Interchange Format maps, 1.6m words, 160,000 claims. Scheme annotation of Walton schemes by trained linguists was found exceptionally difficult.
limits: Survey, not a test. Kappa reading: .61-.80 substantial, .81+ almost perfect (Landis and Koch).
agent_relevance: Gives a shared vocabulary and a common interchange format for the agent's S2 representation.

source: Davies, van Gelder & Barnett: Using computer-assisted argument mapping to teach reasoning
finding: Practitioner method for hidden premises: the Rabbit Rule (a term in the conclusion must appear in a premise) and the Holding Hands Rule (a leftover premise term must pair with a term in another premise). Missing premise gets added as a boxed claim.
numbers: Worked example: premise about Blue Poles, conclusion adds a term not in the premise, so the missing premise is the assumption that Blue Poles does not represent the world.
limits: Teaching text, no accuracy data. Works on simple categorical-style arguments; harder on loose natural prose.
agent_relevance: Directly codeable. A program can check term overlap between conclusion and premises and flag a gap, so the model only writes the missing premise.
quote: No conclusion should come out of thin air. (No rabbits out of hats!)

source: Davies, van Gelder & Barnett: Using computer-assisted argument mapping to teach reasoning
finding: Operational test for linked premises: ask if the conclusion still follows when one premise is missing or false. Premise 3 can support the conclusion without premise 4, but 4 cannot without 3, so 4 is linked to 3.
numbers: Example: Rome is beautiful (independent) versus visiting relatives (linked pair).
limits: Test needs a judgement of whether support remains, which is itself soft; students find the distinction hard.
agent_relevance: A removal test is a good counted check: drop each premise, re-ask if the claim still holds, record the pattern.
quote: If one premise can't support a conclusion without another premise, they are said to be linked

source: Davies, van Gelder & Barnett: Using computer-assisted argument mapping to teach reasoning
finding: Claim that intensive argument-mapping courses raise critical thinking scores about 0.8 standard deviations, more than twice a typical critical thinking course. Source is van Gelder (2015).
numbers: 0.8 SD for high-intensity mapping versus about 0.34 SD typical (the 0.34 figure comes from a search snippet citing Alvarez, not opened).
limits: Secondary report. A search snippet also says Twardy suspected founder effects inflate the 0.8. Gains were measured on tests taken without maps, so it is transfer.
agent_relevance: Weak support for diagramming as a training tool for humans. Says nothing about LLMs.

source: Habernal et al. (2018) The Argument Reasoning Comprehension Task
finding: Task built on Toulmin: given reason and claim, pick the right warrant from two opposing warrants. Crowdsourced in 8 steps from news comment debates.
numbers: 1,970 instances from 2,884 comments. Stance kappa .58 with 5 workers per item at MACE threshold 0.95.
limits: Warrant versus premise is itself contested: van Eemeren et al. say the line holds only in Toulmin's examples. Paper says a warrant can be treated as a linked premise (Freeman).
agent_relevance: Hidden-premise recovery can be tested as a two-choice task. Good for a cheap probe of S2.

source: Habernal et al. (2018) The Argument Reasoning Comprehension Task
finding: Humans do well; early neural models near chance.
numbers: Human average .798 (SD .162); humans with reasoning training .909 (SD .114); 30 of 173 participants scored 100%. Random .473. Best system (intra-warrant attention w/ context) test .556; dev .638. Topic familiarity had no significant effect.
limits: 173 participants; each answered 10 questions. Training in reasoning raised score; general education did not.
agent_relevance: Reasoning training, not world knowledge, separates good from poor at warrants. A scaffold giving a procedure may help.

source: Niven & Kao (2019) Probing neural network comprehension of natural language arguments
finding: BERT's apparent success on ARCT came from cues, not argument understanding. A failed-replication style result.
numbers: BERT Large peak 77% test (human 80%). Warrants alone gave 71% peak. Reason+warrant added 4 points, claim+warrant 2. Word 'not' in the warrant predicts label 61% of the time. On adversarial set (claim negated, warrants swapped) BERT peak fell to 53%, mean and median 50%. 5 of 20 seeds failed to train.
limits: One model family and one dataset; adversarial set built by one native speaker negating claims.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a hidden-premise score without an adversarial control. For our agent: test a restatement by flipping the claim and checking the grounds no longer fit.
quote: BERT's peak performance of 77% on the Argument Reasoning Comprehension Task reaches just three points below the average untrained human baseline

source: Chen, Cheng, Luu, Bing (2023) Exploring the potential of large language models in computational argumentation
finding: Zero-shot GPT-3.5-Turbo, Flan-UL2 and Llama-2 tested on claim, evidence and stance detection. Models beat random on binary tasks but weak on multi-class.
numbers: Claim detection IBM Claims acc: GPT-3.5 72.0, Flan-UL2 74.8, Llama-2-13B 36.0, random 50.2. IAM Claims: 68.2, 83.8, 44.8. IBM Argument: 55.8 / 63.6 (GPT-3.5 p=0.16 not significant). Evidence classification (AQE): GPT-3.5 73.4, Flan-UL2 68.6, Llama-13B 5.2. Under 10 shots LLMs matched BERT-type models trained on 500 samples.
limits: Old models; test sets of 500; Llama-2-13B below random on most tasks.
agent_relevance: Early LLM floor. Multi-class labelling is where small models broke, so keep label sets small.

source: Cabessa, Hernault, Mushtaq (2024) In-context learning and fine-tuning GPT for argument mining
finding: Argument type classification (major claim, claim, premise) on the persuasive-essay corpus. GPT-4 with kNN-picked examples and majority-vote ensembling does well without training; fine-tuned GPT-3.5 beats prior best.
numbers: GPT-4 ICL (5NN, 3-ensemble) macro F1 0.836 (MC .914, C .698, P .897); prior Stab & Gurevych .826, Potash .849, Kuribayashi .856. Fine-tuned GPT-3.5 passes the .857 state of the art. Adding explicit structural features hurt ICL (.821 versus .836).
limits: Claims are the weak class (about .69). Fine-tuning beat ICL, so some task learning still needed.
agent_relevance: Few-shot labelling of claim versus premise reaches near human skill. Claim remains the hard class (human alpha .524).

source: Gorur, Rago, Toni (2024) Can LLMs perform relation-based argument mining?
finding: Binary support/attack between two texts across ten datasets. Large open LLMs beat the RoBERTa baseline.
numbers: Macro F1: Llama-70B-4bit 75, Mixtral-8x7B-4bit 73, Mistral-7B 70, RoBERTa 68, Llama-13B 62-64. Microtexts: RoBERTa 67 vs Llama-70B 96. Essays support/attack/both: RoBERTa 85/38/80, Llama-70B 94/52/90. Attack F1 lower than support almost everywhere. Inference 1.73 s per pair for 70B vs 0.005 s RoBERTa.
limits: Binary only (real use is ternary with no-relation); quantised models; English only; no fine-tuning. Table text extraction was messy; figures read with some alignment risk.
agent_relevance: Pair judgement of support is easy for LLMs; attack is harder. Cost of a big model per pair matters.

source: Gampel et al. (2026) A comprehensive study of LLM-based argument classification: Llama through DeepSeek to GPT-5.2
finding: Stance-style argument classification (for/against a topic) on UKP and Args.me. Voting and rephrasing give a few points; failures are shared across models.
numbers: GPT-5.2 accuracy 78.0% (UKP) and 91.9% (Args.me). Prior BERT 71.6 (UKP F1) and 80.8 (Args.me). Voting gain: Simple +4.4 / +2.6, Tiebreak +4.5 / +2.8, Weighted +2.4 / +2.9 points (UKP / Args.me). Prompt tweaks and certainty gave 2-8 points. CoT helped a few points on UKP, hurt on Args.me.
limits: This is stance classification, not component or structure extraction. Sample trimmed. Shared failure: implicit criticism, complex structure, aligning argument to a claim. Table rows were garbled in text extraction, so the per-model mapping is unsure.
agent_relevance: Same-model voting helps a little, but failures are correlated across models (fits G4). CoT is not a sure gain.

source: Feng & Hunter (2026) Making implicit premises explicit in logical understanding of enthymemes
finding: DeepSeek v3.2 writes 1 to 3 intermediate premises; text is turned into logic via AMR and a SAT solver checks entailment. More generated steps give more entailment accuracy.
numbers: Entailment accuracy (250 items each). ANLI: none .496, original .520, 1-step .624, 2-step .660, 3-step .716. ARCT: none .276, original .292, 1-step .480, 2-step .496, 3-step .560. Best entailment F1 ARCT: original .21 vs 3-step .58.
limits: Only two fixed candidates are classified; not free generation. Depends on AMR parse and 25 hand templates; rows where premise alone entails were skipped; thresholds tuned on the same pool.
agent_relevance: Filling the gap with several explicit bridging steps helps a checker; the check is code, not model opinion (fits G5).

source: Feng & Hunter (2026) Identifying implicit premises for logical reconstruction of argument graphs
finding: On the Microtext Argumentative Corpus (112 texts, 576 segments), generated implicit premises raise three-way relation classification (entailment, contradiction, neutral).
numbers: 420 items (140 per class). No implicit premise: peak accuracy 0.426. One premise: 0.512. Chain of up to 5 steps: 0.555, peak at 4 steps, slight drop at 5. Chance 0.333. Contradiction recall .31 to .52; entailment precision .44 to .51.
limits: Still weak in absolute terms; neutral recall fixed at .63 since no premises generated for it; sixth step often repeats the claim and was dropped.
agent_relevance: Gains are real but modest, and more steps past four hurt. Cap chain length and cut steps that restate the claim.

source: Feng & Hunter (2026) Making implicit premises explicit (prompt design)
finding: Prompt design: ask for a helpful chain and a non-helpful chain, each statement under 10 words, no pronouns. Hidden-premise generation used as a bounded slot.
numbers: Helpful and non-helpful chains of 1, 2, 3 statements per item; ARCT and ANLI augmented offline.
limits: Authors state they did not test alternative template wording.
agent_relevance: Template for the agent's hidden-premise slot: short statements, no pronouns, one explicit chain.

source: Sviridova, Cabrio, Villata (2025) Mining implicit arguments for reasoning: a survey
finding: Cited by 2026 papers as a survey of implicit-argument mining, enthymeme detection and decoding.
numbers: Not opened; only known from reference lists in Feng & Hunter.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Candidate for angle B or a follow-up read.

source: Toulmin (1958) The Uses of Argument
finding: Argument layout: claim, grounds (data), warrant, backing, qualifier, rebuttal. Warrant licenses the step from grounds to claim and is usually implicit.
numbers: Not opened (book). Layout as described in Habernal et al. 2018 and Lawrence & Reed 2019.
limits: Book not read this session. Critics (van Eemeren et al. 1987, cited in Habernal) say warrant versus premise is hard to tell in practice.
agent_relevance: Source of the claim-grounds-warrant restatement for S2.

source: Freeman (2011) Argument Structure: Representation and Theory
finding: Theory of linked versus convergent support; shows the traditional linked definition is ambiguous and allows a warrant to be treated as a linked premise.
numbers: Not opened; position taken from Stab & Gurevych and Habernal et al. citing Freeman 2011.
limits: Book not read.
agent_relevance: Background for representation choices.

source: Johnson & Blair (1977/2006) Logical Self-Defense
finding: Informal logic standard: premise relevance, sufficiency, acceptability (RSA) criteria for good arguments.
numbers: Not opened; stated from general knowledge, no numbers here.
limits: Not verified this session.
agent_relevance: RSA could structure a post-restatement check but must be tested.

source: Peldszus & Stede (2013) From argument diagrams to argumentation mining in texts: a survey
finding: Reviews diagramming schemes (Beardsley, Freeman, Toulmin) and links them to mining tasks.
numbers: PDF not retrievable; only abstract-level info via search.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Source for diagram types if later retrieved.

source: Peldszus & Stede (2016) An annotated corpus of argumentative microtexts
finding: 112 short texts, 576 segments annotated with central claim, premises, support, rebuttal and undercut.
numbers: Counts read via Feng & Hunter 2026 (arXiv 2608.18821), not from the original.
limits: Original not opened.
agent_relevance: Small, clean test bed for restatement checks.

source: Twardy (2004) Argument maps improve critical thinking
finding: Study of argument-mapping training and critical thinking gains.
numbers: Page blocked (HTTP 403). Search snippet only: Twardy reported effects slightly under van Gelder's average of about 0.8 SD and flagged possible founder effects.
limits: Not opened; snippet only.
agent_relevance: Do not cite numbers until read.
